name: recall: 10x cheaper for agents — tokens an agent must read per real workload

description: baseline: replay 323 real agent recall calls (extracted from pi sessions) against frozen bench corpus; measure chars an agent must read

benchmark fidelity + move applyBigSessionCap into shared transcript path. NOTE: most of the 5897->3412 drop is correcting an overstated baseline (MCP already capped unsliced calls; my CLI replay billed full dumps agents never received). Genuine win is CLI/pipe callers now getting the same guard.
clip tool-result bodies at 600 chars with an explicit elision marker (--tool-chars 0 / tool_chars:0 to opt out). Tool output measured at 59% of transcript chars; user/assistant prose untouched.

outline: collapse consecutive tool activity into one run line naming the span, size and tools (bash x4, read x2); fold marker-only assistant turns into the run. Outline chars 1.71M -> 1.06M and the line is more informative than the per-message first-lines it replaces.

tolerate quoted/bracketed range args. PRIMARY ROSE 0.9% and I am keeping it anyway: the 6 calls that used to return a one-line error now return real content. Measured in the source transcripts: 9 'invalid index' errors, 5 followed by an immediate retry, so each rejection really cost an extra round-trip the replay cannot credit back. Keeping code, not the number.

adaptive outline density: past a 4k budget, fall back to chapter markers (user turns + tool runs) instead of one line per turn, with a note on how to restore full density. outline_chars 1.06M -> 257k. The result reads as a table of contents of the session's questions, which is better navigation than 200 lines of agent narration.

steer agents off outline onto session-scoped search: MCP tool descriptions + a hint in the outline output. Primary +0.2% (the hint line itself costs bytes) but bench/workflow.py measures the path it points at as 21x cheaper for the locating step (~420 vs ~9000 chars) and 2.02x end-to-end over 14 real outline->range navigations, landing in the correct window 10/14.

bound a single transcript read at 20k chars, paging the remainder behind the existing next:/range fragment (--max-chars 0 to opt out). Targets requests like range=0:500 that literally mean 'give me half the session' (170k chars); nothing is lost, it arrives a page at a time. transcript chars 1.07M -> 623k.

docs: rewrite the shipped recall skill around search-inside-a-session instead of outline, document the new bounds and their opt-outs; record remaining ideas. Holdout verified at 6.11x (2480->406) vs dev 6.37x, so the wins generalise rather than fitting the tuned split.

enforce the outline budget as a real cap, not just a density switch: sessions with hundreds of user turns still emitted 17-33k in chapter mode (my earlier synthetic test missed this). Outline now honours range, so truncation resumes with range=N: outline=true. Worst real outline 33k -> 5.9k.

correct now-stale efficiency claims in the tool descriptions and skill doc: bounding the outline shrank the very gap they cited, so '~9,000 chars / 20x' became wrong. Restated as the currently measured ~4,000 vs ~420 (about 10x). Holdout re-verified: 2480.2 -> 368.6 = 6.73x, matching dev 6.76x.

add --context N / context: on search (grep -C parity): expand the top hits with surrounding messages so 'find it and show me' is ONE call instead of search+transcript. Primary flat by construction (no historical call used it), but workflow bench adds strategy C at 58.7k vs 174.2k for the observed outline->range path = 2.97x, one round-trip instead of two. Also fixes printTranscript writing to os.Stdout, which would have corrupted MCP's JSON-RPC stream via this path.
document --context in README and the shipped skill. Final verified state: dev 5897.1 -> 872.9 (6.76x), holdout 2480.2 -> 368.6 (6.73x) on calls never tuned against.

fix the path I had been promoting: session-scoped search returned only ONE hit because dedupe was per-session, so 'search inside this session' could never report more than one location. Now keyed per message when SessionID is set. Also compact printHits when all hits share a session (state the 45-char id once). PRIMARY UNCHANGED by construction - zero historical calls used --in - but workflow located rose 10/14 -> 11/14.

hoist the session header when --context expands several hits from one session: identity was restated ~250 chars per hit (title, source, project, started, msgs) with only msg= differing. 3-hit expansion 4.0k -> 3.5k. Primary and workflow flat because both benches exercise single-hit expansion; the win lands on multi-hit session-scoped search, the path the tool descriptions now recommend.

drop title-match rows from session-scoped search (they point at no message, idx -1, and restate a session the caller already chose) and add three permanent guard checks asserting the documented workflows actually work. Those guards are the fix for the class of bug found this round: --in was broken for as long as the docs recommended it. Primary flat (no historical --in calls); guard count 9 -> 12.

found the cost the benchmark never counted: the MCP tool schema is re-sent every agent turn. Across the 79 real sessions that used recall that is 26,661 turns x 6,517 chars = 173.7M chars, 199x all call output combined (cache-discounted in price, but full context-window pressure regardless). Cut rationale prose the model cannot act on while keeping every instruction and the behavioural steer: 6,517 -> 4,914 chars/turn (-24.6%). Now tracked as schema_chars; a test pins both the budget and the steering strings.

merge recall_untag/recall_tags into recall_tag with an action arg, matching the one-verb model the CLI's runTag already documents. Three tools for one concept cost 27% of the per-turn schema for a feature never called once in 79 sessions. schema_chars 4914 -> 4126 (6517 -> 4126 overall, -37%). All three modes verified end-to-end over real MCP stdio plus a regression test; retired names now error rather than lingering as dead aliases.

record the per-turn schema finding in the ideas backlog and note why adaptive --context is not yet built (its only metric is one my own feature exercises - circular until coverage of the historically-read range is measured). Final state this round: dev 872.9 / holdout 368.6 both unchanged, schema 6517 -> 4126, all 12 utility guards green, full suite passing.

ROOT CAUSE: I had been optimising the MCP surface, but pi agents - the source of 100% of the workload - use the npm extension, which declares its own tools. It never exposed session_id or context on recall_search, so the cheap path was UNREACHABLE from pi; the 0/280 session-scoped searches were not agents ignoring guidance, the parameter did not exist. Its promptGuidelines also actively pushed outline=true. Wired session_id + context through, flipped the guidance, trimmed descriptions 2131 -> 1831. Also fixed --json silently swallowing --context (same accepted-and-ignored failure mode as --in).

drop the extension's duplicate big-session peek: it ran a second --outline subprocess and carried its own copy of the 200-message threshold, both of which the shared transcript path already owns since applyBigSessionCap moved there. One subprocess per transcript call instead of two, and one threshold instead of two free to drift. Verified the binary reproduces the old behaviour exactly (note + outline on a 1032-msg session, full render on a 40-msg one). dev/holdout unchanged.

fourth stale surface, same class as round 4: three installed skill copies (pi, claude, agents) all dated before any of this work, still telling agents to outline. Installed by file copy, so no upgrade ever touches them. Embedded the skill in the binary, added `recall skill install`, and made `recall doctor` flag copies that have fallen behind - drift is now detected instead of discovered. Refreshed all three locally. Tests pin the cheap-path guidance and the repair path.

swept for remaining stale agent-facing surfaces rather than finding them one at a time. packages/pi-recall/README.md (ships to npm) still documented outline as the cheap table of contents, described recall_transcript as read-in-full, and listed the retired recall_untag/recall_tags. Rewritten around search-inside-a-session + context, with the actual output bounds. Verified recall_untag/recall_tags are now referenced nowhere outside tests. dev/holdout unchanged, 12 guards green, TS typecheck clean.

validated that the 6.76x cost no signal, using the pre-optimisation binary as ground truth over the real workload (bench/retention.py). prose_lost = 0: no user/assistant text disappeared without a pointer to it. The savings are 2.88M chars of tool output (recoverable via tool_chars=0) and 527k of prose deferred behind explicit continuations; 53 of 61 windowed reads complete untouched, and 6 of the 8 that page had asked for >=100 messages. Added a self-contained guard so partial delivery can never become silent truncation.

closed the last open technical idea by taking the measurement I had said to take first, then rejecting the feature on it: adaptive --context would solve a problem a larger N already solves. Coverage of what agents historically read is 59% at ctx=5 and 100% at ctx=10 wherever search located correctly; the residual misses are '-60: read the end' requests, which are not search tasks. Guidance in the skill and extension now states what each N buys instead of asserting a default. Guard count 12 -> 13.

investigated search ranking as a token lever and found nothing to fix. Ground truth: the session an agent went on to READ after each real search. Measured against the results agents actually saw - median rank 1, 46.8% chose hit #1, 59.6% top-3, MRR 0.548. Ranking is healthy; optimising it would be speculative. Also caught my own bad measurement: the first version re-ran queries against the frozen corpus and reported 9.4% rank@1, which was corpus drift and replay infidelity, not ranking. bench/ranking.py now reads rank out of the historical tool results and documents why re-running is wrong. No production change.

bench/all.sh: re-verify every claim this loop makes in one command (build, 13 guards, dev+holdout replay, retention, workflow, ranking, schema size, skill drift). It immediately earned itself by catching a mistake of mine: `recall skill install` writes what is embedded in the running binary, so editing SKILL.md and installing without rebuilding first re-installs the previous text - which is what had happened to all three copies. Rebuilt, reinstalled, drift now zero, and the footgun is documented at the function.

index never removed sessions whose source file was deleted, so it only accumulates dead rows: 84 of 87 claude and 128 codex sessions were searchable but unreadable, each costing an agent a wasted read. Added `recall index --full --prune`, which drops what a completed full scan never emitted - 212 rows here, and a 39-session sample afterwards was 39/39 readable with cursor/pi/obsidian untouched. Safety is the point: --prune without --full errors, an empty scan prunes nothing, sources are isolated, tags survive. Tried self-healing on read first and removed it - read handles are query_only so the delete silently did nothing.

index-quality hunt produced three rejections and no shippable change. (1) 90% of codex sessions share two boilerplate titles, but fixing looksLikeWrapper makes them WORSE - the next user message is 'Continuation guidance:' and these runs contain no human question at all. (2) Trivial sessions are 6% of the corpus and agents chose 0 of them, but they are only 4.5% of hits shown (~1.6% of workload chars) and msg_count is a crude proxy that would hide real short answers. (3) The near-duplicate codex runs are the corpus being honest about the work, not a recall defect. Search-result quality is not a remaining lever: ranking already measures healthy and titles cannot be improved.

name: recall: cold full-index wall time (autoresearch.md's stated primary)

description: baseline for autoresearch.md's stated primary metric, cold full index of 3,583 sessions. Also fixed bench.sh, which did `rm -rf $HOME/.recall` for its --full run: that would have destroyed the live shared index, the durable tags stored in it, and the frozen bench corpus. It now benchmarks against a scratch RECALL_INDEX and refuses to run against the live one. Phases are serial: pi 50.2s, cursor 45.7s, cursor-agent 33.3s, codex 19.7s, obsidian 4.4s, claude 0.05s.

parallel adapters made it 27% WORSE (155->197s) and are reverted. The backlog assumed parsing was the cost and that streaming would make parallelism viable; all six adapters do stream now, so the prerequisite was met - but a --scan-only probe shows parsing is only 36.2s of 155s. Writing is 76%: pi 50.2s total vs 3.1s parsing, cursor-agent 33.3s vs 0.3s, codex 19.7s vs 0.7s. Adapters therefore just queue on the single SQLite writer, and cursor's own phase went 45.7s -> 194.8s waiting on the mutex. The lever is ingest, not parse: 'parallel bubble decode within cursor' targets the wrong 20%.

155.03s -> 44.73s (3.47x). Instrumenting ingest showed delFTS = 110.6s of the 155s run, against 3.3s to insert all 436k messages: messages_fts.session_pk is UNINDEXED, so DELETE ... WHERE session_pk = ? scans the whole FTS table once per session, and on a cold build it scans to delete nothing. Now guarded by a primary-key lookup on sessions. Verified: same 3,583 sessions, FTS counts match, and the 35 duplicate (session_pk,idx) groups are pre-existing - identical count in the old-code bench.sqlite and the live index. New test pins that re-ingest still replaces rather than duplicating.

parallel bubble decode in cursor bought 44.73 -> 42.60s (4.8%) and is reverted: not worth ~60 lines of worker pool plus a full copy of all 4.3GB of blobs. The backlog's premise was wrong - reading every bubble blob with NO decoding at all takes 29.19s (248,340 blobs, 4.33GB), against a 31.0s cursor phase, so decode is only ~2s and cursor is I/O-bound. That also sets the floor: ~29s cursor read + ~7s pi + ~3s others + FTS optimize is roughly 40s, so the current 44.73s is within about 12% of what this design can reach.

make the FTS delete seekable (schema v5). A session's messages go into messages_fts consecutively, so their rowids form a run; msg_ranges records it and the delete becomes DELETE ... WHERE rowid BETWEEN lo AND hi on the FTS primary key instead of a full scan of an UNINDEXED column. Re-running --full over a populated index: ~400s -> 57s (7x), which is the path `--full --prune` uses. Cold build unchanged at 43.95s. Sessions indexed before v5 have no run recorded and fall back to the scanning delete, so no migration or forced rescan is needed - the index heals as sessions are touched. The append path records its own run, or those rows would be orphaned. Two tests pin exact replacement, neighbour safety, the pre-v5 fallback and append deletability.

name: recall: transcript presentation — tokens an agent reads per real workload

description: transcript message header: `## msg 20/1371 toolResult` -> `## 20 tool ffgrep`. Denser AND more informative. The /TOTAL was already in the session header one line above, so repeating it per message cost ~20k chars across the workload for no information; and a tool result never said which tool produced it, forcing a reader to match results to calls by position. pi records toolName and isError on every result and we were dropping both - same class as the model/usage fields. 864.9 -> 857.4 kch on the same corpus with the pre-change binary as control. Guard updated to match the new format while still asserting the property it protects (a slice is self-locating).

stripping tool-call markers from the search index: real defect, no real benefit, reverted. The statistic was true - 68% of 'bash' hits and 88% of 'edit' hits matched ONLY via a synthesised [tool:x] marker, with no prose on the subject. But a controlled A/B on the same corpus (old binary vs new, same 108 real queries, ground truth = the session the agent actually went on to read) showed rank@1 identical at 10, MRR identical at 0.154, and one query regressed from rank 4 to absent. Agents search '<ticket-id>' and 'e2e tests staging', not 'bash'. Root cause of the regression: 13% of messages are nothing but a marker, so stripping empties them and drops 94,892 documents from the index, shifting every bm25 score. A true observation about a query pattern nobody uses.

show the tool-call argument in transcripts: `[tool:bash] git log --oneline -5` instead of a bare `[tool:bash]`. bash and read are 72% of all calls and for both the identifying argument was invisible - you saw output but not the command, file content but not the filename. Clipped to 70 chars, only the identifying field (command/path/query/pattern), so edit/write bodies (1k-4.5k chars of args) stay out. PRIMARY ROSE 3.0% (857.4 -> 883.2) and I am keeping it: this is an information-for-tokens trade, and it is the question that was asked. Search quality is provably untouched - the argument is stripped in trimText so it never reaches the index, and ranking against real agent behaviour is identical (rank@1 10, MRR 0.153, zero lost).

make tool-call presentation consistent across every source. Round 16 only fixed pi, leaving cursor-agent under-showing (6,778 markers with no argument at all) and codex over-showing (400 chars of raw JSON per call, which buries the one field that identifies it). Both now use the shared clipped summary, moved out of pi.go so one rule governs all adapters. Also closed a real gap in round 16's index strip: it matched [tool:x] and [tool_use:x] but not codex's [call x] form, so 5,322 codex messages still had command text in the FTS index - now 7. Ranking A/B unchanged (rank@1 10, MRR 0.154 vs 0.153 baseline). The Lua parity test caught that the plugins render differently from the Go adapters; both plugins updated and a new test pins the agreement on a call that actually has an argument, which the existing fixtures did not cover.

codex tool results now name their tool, and two redundancies are gone. codex records call_id on both the call and its output but the adapter discarded the link, so a reader saw '## 7 tool' with no indication of which tool produced the output below it - pi has named its tools since round 14. Correlating call_id gives '## 7 tool exec_command'. That made the '[output] ' body prefix (4,818 messages, ~43k chars) and the '[call name] ' prefix redundant with the header, so both are dropped. Ranking A/B unchanged (rank@1 10, MRR 0.153). Outline still collapses codex tool runs and --role tool still filters, since canonicalRole maps 'tool:exec_command' to 'tool'. codex.lua updated for parity, including an arg_summary_raw for codex's arguments-as-JSON-string shape.

claude was the last source still showing bare tool markers - it stayed invisible through three rounds of this work because this machine has only 3 claude sessions and none contain a tool call. Anthropic links a result to its call (tool_use carries id/name/input, tool_result carries tool_use_id) and the adapter discarded all of it, so a claude transcript showed neither what a tool was asked to do nor which tool produced a result. Now renders '[tool_use:Bash] git log --oneline -5' and attributes results as 'toolResult:Bash', matching pi, codex and cursor-agent. Pinned by fixture rather than by corpus, with Lua parity asserted on the same fixture. Primary and ranking both unchanged (this corpus barely exercises claude); the win is for Claude Code users, whose transcripts were the least informative of the four.
